title: Aftermath and Wardrobe
premise: Isandro Okafor, once a piano prodigy whose career ended in a scandal no one will name aloud, has spent eleven years invisible as a janitor at the conservatory that made them. When the group home where they grew up is scheduled for auction and demolition, Isandro returns to salvage what they can and finds a box of photographs and letters implicating Maestro Aldous Renner—the man who 'discovered' them—in abuses that touched every child in his care. As the auction date approaches, Isandro must decide whether to stay silent and safe or testify to a truth that will cost them their last refuge. The novel ends with Isandro choosing to speak at the public hearing, forgiving not Renner but the child they once were, as the wrecking ball falls on schedule and they walk out carrying nothing but a single photograph.
about_author: Juniper Oyelaran is a former music teacher who left the conservatory world after a decade and now writes about institutions, memory, and the people who clean up after greatness. They live in Lagos and Lisbon, dividing their time between both cities and an aging upright piano they refuse to tune.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Working the night shift at the conservatory, Isandro catalogs the building's secrets—scratched doors, hidden cigarettes—as easily as their own silences. A notice on the bulletin board announces the auction of St. Ambrose Children's Home. The emotional beat is controlled dread: the past has found an address.

chapters.title: The Prodigy Who Sweeps
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, with flashbacks. A young violinist, Tamsin, recognizes Isandro from old recital footage and asks why they quit. Isandro deflects with practiced charm, but the question lodges. We learn fragments of the scandal through what Isandro refuses to say. Emotional beat: the cost of being recognized.

chapters.title: Lot 47
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. At the pre-auction viewing, Isandro walks the condemned home, touching doorframes measured in pencil heights. They find a locked supply closet still holding Renner's donated piano and a shoebox of photographs—children posed beside the maestro, some faces circled in red ink. Beat: grief sharpening into suspicion.

chapters.title: The Stranger in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Studying the photos at night, Isandro identifies themselves at age nine, standing too close to Renner, smiling the smile of a child who has learned performance as survival. Another former resident, Bex, calls after seeing the auction listing; her voice cracks when Isandro mentions the box. Beat: the first crack in eleven years of silence.

chapters.title: What the Letters Wanted
chapters.summary: Bex's POV. Bex arrives unannounced and reveals she wrote letters to the diocese years ago—letters that were buried by a lawyer now running for office. She wants Isandro to co-sign a statement before the hearing that could delay demolition. Isandro refuses. Beat: two survivors pulling in opposite directions.

chapters.title: Practice Room Six
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Isandro confronts Renner, now frail and celebrated, during his final masterclass. The conversation is oblique, courteous, devastating—Renner remembers everything except guilt. He offers Isandro a letter of recommendation, as if buying silence with paper. Beat: power's banality; Isandro nearly accepts.

chapters.title: Auction Day
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. The home sells to a developer within minutes. Watching strangers carry out beds and hymnals, Isandro realizes the building was never the sanctuary—survival was, and survival has its own debts. Tamsin appears, having researched the scandal herself, and asks directly: was it him? Beat: cornered by kindness.

chapters.title: The Weight of a Signature
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV, long night. Isandro drafts and burns three versions of a testimony, then plays Renner's abandoned piano for the first time since childhood—the hands remember what the mind surrendered. They call Bex at dawn. Beat: the turning point, chosen rather than forced.

chapters.title: Hearing
chapters.summary: Alternating Isandro and Bex POV. At the public preservation hearing, Isandro testifies—not to stop the demolition but to make the record true, naming Renner and the institution that protected him. Renner's lawyer circles; the room splits between disbelief and recognition. Beat: climax—justice spoken outside any courtroom, at personal ruin.

chapters.title: Aftermath and Wardrobe
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Demolition day. Isandro salvages one photograph—young self, uncircled—and donates the rest and the letters to an archive Bex found. They resign from the conservatory, keep the janitor's keys as a talisman, and finally play in public, badly and gladly, at a neighborhood hall. Beat: forgiveness of the stranger in the photo; freedom without absolution.
